Physical pain in a part of the body

vignette:
Miguel is a 53-year-old tax consultant who, eighteen months ago, was walking home from a downtown office when he came upon two police officers beating a young Latino man on the sidewalk. The man’s face was bloody, his arm twisted at an unnatural angle. Miguel tried to shout for them to stop; an officer shoved him hard to the ground, wrenching Miguel’s shoulder. The officers finally dragged the young man away, leaving Miguel kneeling on the pavement, his arm throbbing, the image of the victim’s injuries seared into his mind. In the days that followed, he found himself replaying that moment and arriving at a terrible conclusion: something about him—his presence, his failure to act more forcefully—had made it happen. That belief took root and never loosened.

Within weeks, Miguel began avoiding unfamiliar neighborhoods entirely, certain he could not assess the danger in places he did not know. At work, he planned escape routes in every new meeting room before he could sit down, and he started checking behind him constantly on the walk to his car. The more he scanned his surroundings, the more he noticed other people’s visible injuries—a bandaged hand, a bruised cheek—and each sighting sent him back into the old loop: he felt isolated and set apart, as if he carried a stain that others could see. The physical pain in his shoulder, which flared unpredictably, became an immediate reminder of his intrinsic fault; once it started, he would think, This is proof that I deserved it, that my life isn’t worth continuing. His vigilance then intensified further—he would look behind him more often, recalculate his exits—and his hopelessness deepened: the very act of checking confirmed for him that the world was dangerous and that he, alone, was the flawed one.

His occupation made these patterns inescapable. As a tax consultant, Miguel had always met clients in their own offices, but now he refused any appointment in a part of town he had not visited before. Colleagues noticed his reluctance and stopped inviting him to team lunches; he began eating alone at his desk, where he could keep his back to the wall and watch the door. The isolation he felt became a self-fulfilling prophecy. He stopped returning calls from his adult children, convinced they would see the shame in him. The days blurred into a routine of work, scanning, and silent despair.

What finally brought Miguel to a clinic was the weight of the constant surveillance. He could no longer go to the grocery store without mapping every aisle for exits, and a recent flare of shoulder pain had sent him into a three-day spiral of suicidal thinking. He made an appointment because he could no longer bear the loop—but he also feared that no one could understand the truth he carried: that the event happened because of who he was. He sat in the waiting room with his back to the wall, already planning how he would leave.
